lessonTitle: The Ideal Gas Model: Equation of State and Specific Heats

blocks.text: A hospital oxygen cylinder is marked with its volume and a gauge pressure, and the supplier must decide how many kilograms of gas it holds before it is shipped. The ideal gas model turns a pressure, a volume and a temperature into a mass with one equation, but only if the gas is far from condensing.

blocks.markdown: The **ideal gas model** treats the molecules as points with no mutual attraction. It gives the equation of state relating pressure $p$ (kPa, absolute), volume $V$ (m$^3$), mass $m$ (kg) and temperature $T$ (K):

blocks.caption: $v=V/m$ is specific volume in m$^3$/kg; $R$ is the specific gas constant in kJ/(kg K), $R=R_u/M$ with $R_u=8.314$ kJ/(kmol K) and $M$ the molar mass
Typical values near room temperature; the specific heats vary with temperature

blocks.title: Mass of air in a rigid tank
blocks.prompt: A rigid tank of volume 2.0 m$^3$ holds air at 500 kPa absolute and 300 K. Treating air as an ideal gas with R = 0.287 kJ/(kg K), find the mass.
blocks.answer: The tank holds about 11.6 kg of air. Always use absolute pressure and kelvin.

blocks.markdown: The ideal gas has two specific heats: $c_v$ at constant volume and $c_p$ at constant pressure. Since $h=u+pv=u+RT$, differentiating with respect to temperature gives a fixed link between them:

blocks.caption: $k$ is the specific heat ratio (dimensionless); with $R$ known, either specific heat gives the other

blocks.title: Why cp exceeds cv
blocks.text: At constant pressure the gas must also push back its surroundings as it expands, so it takes more heat to raise the temperature by 1 K. The extra heat per kilogram equals the work $R\,\Delta T$.

blocks.title: Specific heats of nitrogen
blocks.prompt: For nitrogen, R = 0.2968 kJ/(kg K) and cp = 1.039 kJ/(kg K). Find cv and the ratio k.
blocks.answer: cv is about 0.742 kJ/(kg K) and k is about 1.40, as expected for a diatomic gas.

blocks.markdown: The model is an approximation. Real gases deviate when molecules are close together (high pressure) or near condensation (low temperature). The **compressibility factor** measures the deviation:

blocks.caption: $Z=1$ for an ideal gas; $Z<1$ means attractive forces dominate, $Z>1$ means repulsion dominates

blocks.title: Is the ideal gas model acceptable?
blocks.prompt: A gas with R = 0.2968 kJ/(kg K) is measured at 8 MPa and 300 K with v = 0.0112 m$^3$/kg. Find Z and judge the model (accept if Z is within about 5 % of 1).

steps.text: Apply the definition with p in kPa.
Compare with 1: Z is within 5 % of 1 (deviation 0.6 %), so the ideal gas model is acceptable for this state.

blocks.answer: Z = 1.006, so the ideal gas model is acceptable here. The 5 % tolerance is a rule of thumb, not a law.

blocks.title: Absolute values only
blocks.text: Pressure in pV = mRT is absolute pressure, not gauge. Temperature is in kelvin. A gauge reading of 300 kPa in a room at 101 kPa means 401 kPa absolute.

blocks.title: When is the model good?
blocks.text: The ideal gas model works at low pressure and at temperatures well above the critical temperature. Air at atmospheric conditions is an excellent case, whereas a vapour near saturation is not.

points: The ideal gas equation pV = mRT uses absolute pressure and kelvin, with R = R_u/M specific to the gas.
The specific heats of an ideal gas satisfy cp - cv = R, and k = cp/cv.
The compressibility factor Z = pv/(RT) measures deviation from ideal behaviour; Z close to 1 means the model is acceptable.
Use the model at low pressure and high temperature relative to the critical point.

questions.stem: Which pair of quantities must be used in pV = mRT?

options.text: Gauge pressure and temperature in degrees Celsius
Absolute pressure and temperature in kelvin
Absolute pressure and temperature in degrees Celsius
Gauge pressure and temperature in kelvin

questions.correctOptionText: Absolute pressure and temperature in kelvin
questions.explanation: The equation of state is derived for absolute scales, so zero pressure and zero temperature must mean the real zero. Gauge or Celsius values introduce an offset that gives a wrong mass.

questions.stem: For an ideal gas, which relation between specific heats is correct?

options.text: cp + cv = R
cv - cp = R
cp - cv = R
cp / cv = R

distractorRationale.a: The difference, not the sum, equals R.
distractorRationale.d: The ratio is k, which is dimensionless.

questions.explanation: Starting from h = u + RT and differentiating with respect to T gives cp = cv + R. The ratio of the two is k and has no units.

questions.stem: A gas at some state has a compressibility factor Z = 0.62. What is the best conclusion?

options.text: The ideal gas model is poor because Z differs greatly from 1
The ideal gas model is acceptable since Z is positive
The gas must be at zero pressure
The gas is above its critical temperature

questions.correctOptionText: The ideal gas model is poor because Z differs greatly from 1

distractorRationale.b: Z must be near 1 for the model.
distractorRationale.c: Z tends to 1 as pressure tends to 0.
distractorRationale.d: Nothing about the critical point follows from Z alone.

questions.explanation: Z = 1 for an ideal gas, so Z = 0.62 means the real specific volume is 38 % below the ideal value and the ideal model would be badly in error. Attractive forces dominate at such a state.

questions.stem: Why does heating an ideal gas by 10 K at constant pressure require more heat per kilogram than heating it by 10 K at constant volume?

options.text: The gas has more molecules at constant pressure
At constant volume the temperature rise is smaller
cv is larger than cp
At constant pressure the gas also does expansion work, equal to R times the temperature rise

questions.correctOptionText: At constant pressure the gas also does expansion work, equal to R times the temperature rise

distractorRationale.a: Mass is the same in both cases.
distractorRationale.b: Both are stated to be 10 K.

questions.explanation: At constant volume all the heat goes into internal energy, but at constant pressure part must also supply the work of expansion. This is why cp = cv + R.

questions.stem: Which of these states is LEAST suited to the ideal gas model?

options.text: Air at 101 kPa and 20 C
Helium at 200 kPa and 300 K
Carbon dioxide at 7.5 MPa and 32 C
Hydrogen at 100 kPa and 500 K

questions.correctOptionText: Carbon dioxide at 7.5 MPa and 32 C

distractorRationale.a: This is the textbook ideal case.
distractorRationale.b: Helium is almost ideal under these conditions.

questions.explanation: CO2 at 7.5 MPa and 32 C lies close to its critical point (about 7.4 MPa and 31 C), where Z is far from 1. The other three states combine low pressure with temperatures far above critical, so intermolecular forces are negligible.

questions.stem: A 12-litre (0.012 m$^3$) cylinder contains air at 10 MPa absolute and 20 C (293.15 K). Treat as an ideal gas with R = 0.287 kJ/(kg K). Find the mass of air in kg.
questions.explanation: m = pV/(RT) = 10000 x 0.012/(0.287 x 293.15) = 1.426 kg. Pressure in kPa and R in kJ/(kg K) give kJ, consistent with p V in kPa m^3.

questions.stem: Helium has cp = 5.193 kJ/(kg K) and a specific gas constant R = 2.077 kJ/(kg K) (typical values). Find cv in kJ/(kg K).
questions.explanation: cv = cp - R = 5.193 - 2.077 = 3.116 kJ/(kg K). The ratio k = 5.193/3.116 = 1.67, typical of a monatomic gas.

questions.stem: Carbon dioxide (R = 0.1889 kJ/(kg K)) at 6 MPa and 350 K has a measured specific volume of 0.0086 m$^3$/kg. Find the compressibility factor Z (dimensionless).
questions.explanation: Z = pv/(RT) = 6000 x 0.0086/(0.1889 x 350) = 0.780. This is well below 1, so the ideal gas model would overestimate the specific volume by roughly 28 %.

questions.stem: Starting from the definition of enthalpy and the ideal gas equation of state, show that cp - cv = R for an ideal gas and explain the physical meaning of the result.
markingGuide: For an ideal gas pv = RT so h = u + RT
Differentiating with respect to T: dh/dT = du/dT + R
cp = dh/dT and cv = du/dT for an ideal gas (u and h functions of T only)
So cp - cv = R, with R in kJ/(kg K)
Meaning: extra heat at constant pressure goes to expansion work
questions.explanation: The step h = u + RT links the two derivatives directly, giving cp = cv + R. Physically, the extra heat needed at constant pressure supplies the work done on the surroundings as the gas expands.

questions.stem: Define the compressibility factor Z and explain how it is used to decide whether a state may be treated as an ideal gas. Give the conditions of pressure and temperature under which Z tends to 1.
markingGuide: Deviation of Z from 1 (for example more than about 5 %) means the model is poor
Z tends to 1 at low pressure
Z tends to 1 at temperatures well above the critical temperature
Mentions intermolecular forces or finite molecular volume as the cause of departure
questions.explanation: Z compares the real specific volume with the ideal one at the same p and T. It approaches 1 when molecules are far apart (low pressure) and move quickly (high temperature), so attractive forces and molecular volume are negligible.
